entries.text: Rot is what wet does to wood. The birch limb by my workbench has gone soft just where it lies on the ground. So maybe his stones are there to hold his square sticks up out of the damp. A guess, until I see more.

entries.text: The stranger came down to his end of the stepping stones with something pale rolled under his arm, looked at my scoop in the water, and stopped. He didn't step on. He just stood there. He dipped his head and came across slow, setting each foot down flat, only one knock, and went off west into the trees toward the boulder, where the sun is.
entries.title: He waited

entries.text: He stood and waited so his feet wouldn't scatter my fish. That's the third time today he's been careful of them. I wonder what he goes west for every evening, with the sun in his face.

entries.text: Just as it got dark a light came bobbing back out of the trees from the west, and it was him, with his lamp. I just watched him go, and I didn't look away.

entries.text: Asked the slate whether taking fish makes fewer. It can: a little pond can be fished down fast, so pond keepers set a limit on how many come out in a year, and a new pond is left alone until its fish have bred. They say take the middle-sized ones and let the biggest go back.

entries.text: So the pool isn't endless, it's more like the acorns under the red oak. One or two a day, and if a big one ever comes into the scoop, it goes back so it can make more. I'll keep count, the way I count hoots.
